content.heading: 1.1  The big shift — from writing steps to stating goals
content.body:
All the software you have written so far is DETERMINISTIC. In Java, if you write a method that adds two numbers, calling it with 2 and 3 gives you 5 — every time, forever. You wrote every rule; the computer follows them exactly. If the program should handle a new situation, you must add code for that situation.

Agentic AI is a different way of building software. Instead of writing out every step, you describe a GOAL and hand the system the ability to figure out the steps itself — including asking your code for help when it needs to.

A simple picture: imagine the difference between a recipe and a cook. A traditional program is a RECIPE — it lists exact steps; follow them and you get the dish, the same way every time. An agentic program is a COOK — you stock the kitchen, name the dish you want, and the cook decides how to make it, tasting and adjusting along the way.

That "cook" is a Large Language Model (an LLM). The "kitchen and ingredients" are the tools you make available. The "tasting and adjusting" is a loop of thinking and acting. This unit is about understanding the cook. Later units are about the kitchen and the loop.
content.callout: A traditional program follows a recipe you wrote. An agentic program is a cook you hand a goal.

content.heading: 1.2  What an LLM is, in plain words
content.body:
A Large Language Model is, at heart, a very large and very well-tuned text-prediction machine. You give it some text, and it produces text that plausibly continues or responds to what you gave it. It learned to do this by being trained on an enormous amount of written material.

Here is the single most important idea in the whole subject, worth reading twice: an LLM predicts the next chunk of text, over and over. That is all it fundamentally does.

Everything an LLM appears to "do" — answer a question, write an essay, plan a trip, produce code — comes out of repeatedly predicting the next most plausible piece of text, given everything that came before. It is not looking things up in a database. It is not running a program in its head. It is continuing text in a statistically sensible way.
content.snippet:
give the model everything so far  ->  it suggests the next tiny piece
add that piece to the text        ->  ask again for the next piece
repeat hundreds of times          ->  a full answer emerges
content.snippetExplanation: What this shows: To produce a sentence, the model does not compose the whole thing at once. It adds one small piece, then reconsiders everything and adds the next — like a person writing one word at a time but only ever thinking about "what comes next." Once you absorb this, the odd behaviors of LLMs stop being mysterious.
content.callout: Because the model is "just" continuing text, it can be astonishingly fluent AND confidently wrong at the same time. Fluency is not truth.

content.heading: 1.3  What LLMs are good and bad at
content.body:
Understanding the strengths and weaknesses of LLMs is the foundation of every design decision in agentic AI.

LLMs are genuinely GOOD at: understanding and producing natural language; transforming text (summarizing, translating, rephrasing, extracting); writing and explaining code; following patterns and examples; "reasoning" over information you place in front of them; and choosing among options you describe (this quietly powers tool use).

LLMs are UNRELIABLE or bad at: facts they did not clearly learn (they invent plausible-sounding falsehoods — "hallucination," the number-one risk); exact arithmetic and careful counting (they predict likely digits rather than calculating); anything current or live (they have a training cutoff); being consistent (the same question can give different answers); and knowing what they do not know.

Here is the central design insight of the whole field, born directly from that list: we let the LLM do what it is good at — understanding, deciding, planning, phrasing — and we hand off what it is bad at — exact facts, math, live data, and taking real actions — to TOOLS: ordinary, reliable code, APIs, databases, calculators.
content.callout: The LLM is the brain that decides; your dependable code does the exact work. That handoff is the essence of agentic AI.

content.heading: 1.4  Chatbot vs agent — the distinction that defines the field
content.body:
People use "chatbot" and "agent" loosely, but they are meaningfully different.

A plain LLM interaction (a CHATBOT): one input goes in, one answer comes out; it takes no actions in the real world; there is no loop and no memory beyond the text you provide. Example: "Summarize this paragraph." You get a summary. Done.

An AGENT is more: it pursues a GOAL across MULTIPLE STEPS; it can TAKE ACTIONS through tools (search, run code, call an API, read or write files); it OBSERVES what those actions return and DECIDES what to do next; and it LOOPS until the goal is met (or it gives up, or it hits a safety limit).

There is a compact way to remember what an agent is: AGENT = LLM + TOOLS + A LOOP + A GOAL. Take away the tools and the loop, and you are back to a chatbot. Add them, and you get something that can fix a bug, research a topic across many sources, or run a multi-step process — deciding each move for itself.
content.snippet:
THE GOAL
   |
   v
THINK   — the LLM decides what to do next        <----+
   |                                                  |
   v                                                  |
ACT     — a tool / API / function is called           |
   |                                                  |
   v                                                  |
OBSERVE — the result is fed back to the LLM  ---------+
   |
   v  (once the goal is met)
ANSWER
content.snippetExplanation: What this shows: This THINK → ACT → OBSERVE cycle, repeated, is the beating heart of every agent you will build. Frameworks dress it up in different clothing, but underneath it is always this same loop.
content.callout: AGENT = LLM + TOOLS + A LOOP + A GOAL. Memorize this; the rest of the book elaborates it.

content.heading: 1.5  A ladder of autonomy
content.body:
"Agent" is not all-or-nothing. It helps to think in LEVELS of autonomy, from a plain answer to a fully self-directed system:

Level 0 — a plain answer ("answer this question").
Level 1 — a reliable, structured reply your code can act on.
Level 2 — one tool use (the model calls one function).
Level 3 — a full agent loop (it loops through tools to reach a goal).
Level 4 — a planning agent (makes a multi-step plan, then works it).
Level 5 — a team of agents cooperating.
Level 6 — long-running autonomy (works over hours or days on its own).

This book climbs the ladder deliberately: early units live near the bottom; later ones reach the top. One principle towers above the rest, and professionals repeat it like a mantra: use the LEAST agentic thing that works. Do not reach for a five-agent swarm when a single call would do. More autonomy means more cost, more waiting, more unpredictability, and more ways to fail.
content.callout: The skill that separates shipping agents from demo agents is choosing the LOWEST level of autonomy that reliably does the job.

content.heading: 1.6  A story to make it concrete
content.body:
Picture an agent with a single tool that can look up the weather. You ask it: "What's the weather in Tokyo, and should I pack an umbrella for tomorrow?"

THINK: The agent reasons, "I can't know tomorrow's weather from memory. I have a weather tool. I should use it."
ACT: It issues a request — look up Tokyo's weather for tomorrow.
(Your code actually calls a weather service and gets back: rain, 80% chance, 18 degrees.)
OBSERVE: That real result is handed back to the agent.
THINK: "An 80% chance of rain clearly means an umbrella. I now have enough to answer."
ANSWER: "Tokyo will be rainy tomorrow — about an 80% chance, around 18°C. Yes, pack an umbrella."

Notice the division of labor, which is the whole philosophy in miniature: the LLM decided WHAT to do, WHEN to stop, and how to phrase the answer; your reliable CODE supplied the actual live fact.
content.callout: Every agent, no matter how elaborate, is an elaboration of this little story.

content.heading: 1.7  Misconceptions to clear up now
content.body:
"The model runs my code." No — the model REQUESTS that a piece of code be run; your own system actually runs it and hands back the result.

"The agent remembers me." Only if you deliberately give it the past conversation again. The model keeps nothing between requests on its own.

"A bigger model is always better." No — smaller, faster models are often better for the many quick decisions inside an agent loop: cheaper, faster, and good enough.

"Agents are magical autonomy." They are loops wrapped around a text predictor. Powerful, but they fail in ordinary ways: looping forever, picking the wrong tool, inventing an argument.

"More agents means more power." More agents means more coordination and more ways to go wrong. Use the fewest that do the job.

"Prompting is just typing nicely." It is a real, disciplined, testable skill.
content.callout: Keep these in mind — most beginner confusion about agents traces back to one of them.

content.heading: Check your understanding
content.body:
These are for reflection, not coding. If you can answer them in your own words, you are ready for the next chapter.

1. In one sentence, explain why an LLM by itself cannot reliably tell you today's date, but an agent can.

2. Restate the formula AGENT = LLM + TOOLS + LOOP + GOAL and describe, in plain words, what each of the four parts contributes.

3. Why does "fluent" not mean "correct" when it comes to LLM output?

4. Take a task you do at work — say, triaging a bug report — and describe it as a THINK / ACT / OBSERVE loop. What tools would the agent need?

5. Explain the principle "use the least agentic thing that works," and why reaching straight for a team of agents is usually a mistake.
content.callout: When these feel easy to answer aloud, move on to Chapter 2 — How LLMs Work.
